title: Interscalene block anesthetizes the phrenic nerve (C3-C5): diaphragm paralysis
vignette: A 55-year-old man is being evaluated for a 4-week history of right shoulder pain. The pain worsens when actively abducting the shoulder or when lying on the shoulder at night. The patient also has weakness with abduction and external rotation of the right shoulder. He has attempted treatment with over-the-counter analgesics with limited relief. MRI of the shoulder shows a partial rotator cuff tear, and the patient is scheduled for surgical repair. Immediately before the surgery, he receives anesthesia with an injection between the right anterior and middle scalene muscles to block the C3 through C7 nerve roots of the cervical and brachial plexuses. Which of the following muscles is most likely to be paralyzed due to the anesthesia?

clues.text: injection between the right anterior and middle scalene muscles
clues.note: Injection into the interscalene groove (between anterior and middle scalene) is an interscalene brachial plexus block for shoulder/upper-arm surgery.

clues.text: block the C3 through C7 nerve roots
clues.note: Anesthetic spreading to the C3-C5 roots affects the PHRENIC nerve (C3-C5), causing ipsilateral diaphragmatic paralysis.

whatMatters: An INTERSCALENE block deposits anesthetic near the C5-C7 brachial plexus roots, but it commonly spreads to the C3-C5 roots that form the PHRENIC NERVE, causing transient IPSILATERAL DIAPHRAGM paralysis. Answer B.
strategy: Recognize the interscalene block and recall its classic complication: phrenic nerve (C3-C5) involvement -> hemidiaphragm paralysis (avoid in severe lung disease/contralateral phrenic palsy). Reject muscles supplied by other nerves: cricothyroid (external branch of superior laryngeal, CN X), intercostals (thoracic ventral rami), platysma (facial nerve CN VII), and sternocleidomastoid (accessory nerve CN XI).

eliminations.label: Cricothyroid - superior laryngeal nerve (CN X)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a laryngeal muscle that tenses the vocal cords. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (CN X), not the C3-C7 roots blocked here. ✅ Correct if: superior laryngeal nerve injury (voice change).

eliminations.label: Intercostal - thoracic ventral rami
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: muscles of the chest wall aiding respiration. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: intercostals are innervated by THORACIC (T1-T11) ventral rami, not the cervical roots in an interscalene block. ✅ Correct if: thoracic spinal nerve involvement.

eliminations.label: Platysma - facial nerve (CN VII)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a superficial neck muscle. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is innervated by the cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), unrelated to the C3-C7 roots. ✅ Correct if: facial nerve involvement.

eliminations.label: Sternocleidomastoid - accessory nerve (CN XI)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: neck muscle controlling head rotation/flexion. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is primarily innervated by the accessory nerve (CN XI) (with C2-C3 sensory), not the blocked plexus roots. ✅ Correct if: accessory nerve injury.

reasoning: Injection between anterior and middle scalene = interscalene brachial plexus block
Anesthetic spreads to the C3-C5 roots that form the phrenic nerve
The phrenic nerve is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm
mechanism: The BRACHIAL PLEXUS arises from the C5-T1 roots, which combine into trunks passing between the ANTERIOR and MIDDLE SCALENE muscles (the interscalene/scalene triangle). An INTERSCALENE NERVE BLOCK deposits anesthetic here to anesthetize the upper plexus (C5-C7) for SHOULDER and upper-arm surgery. Because anesthetic in the interscalene sheath readily spreads to the nearby C3-C5 roots that form the PHRENIC NERVE, it very commonly causes transient IPSILATERAL DIAPHRAGMATIC PARALYSIS ('C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive'). This is usually well tolerated but should be AVOIDED in patients who cannot tolerate unilateral diaphragm paralysis (severe COPD, contralateral phrenic nerve dysfunction). The distractor muscles are supplied by different nerves outside the blocked C3-C7 territory: cricothyroid (superior laryngeal, CN X), intercostals (thoracic ventral rami), platysma (facial, CN VII), and sternocleidomastoid (accessory, CN XI).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Anatomy > brachial plexus & phrenic nerve: plexus (C5-T1) between anterior/middle scalene; interscalene block for shoulder surgery; phrenic nerve C3-C5 ('keeps the diaphragm alive'); block spreads to phrenic -> hemidiaphragm paralysis.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Interscalene block reaches C3-C5 -> phrenic nerve -> ipsilateral diaphragm paralysis.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on interscalene block, brachial plexus roots, phrenic nerve (C3-C5), or scalene triangle? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Cricothyroid = CN X; intercostals = thoracic rami; platysma = CN VII; SCM = CN XI - none are C3-C7 diaphragm supply.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: interscalene block -> phrenic nerve (C3-C5) -> transient hemidiaphragm paralysis; avoid in severe lung disease.
